{{Short description|none}}
This is a '''list of misnamed theorems''' in [[mathematics]]. It includes [[theorem]]s (and [[lemma (mathematics)|lemmas]], corollaries, [[conjecture (mathematics)|conjectures]], laws, and perhaps even the odd object) that are well known in mathematics, but which are not named for the originator. That is, the items on this list illustrate [[Stigler's law of eponymy]] (which is not, of course, due to [[Stephen Stigler]], who credits [[Robert K Merton]]).

Please follow the model of previous entries to see how to do this yourself if you want to add another entry.  PLEASE be careful, since the grammar is sensitive and the tiniest mistake is likely to destroy the formatting of this entire page!  See the talk page for more information -->== Applied mathematics ==
[[File:Rozklad benforda.svg|thumb|Benford's law]]
*[[Benford's law]]. This was first stated in 1881 by [[Simon Newcomb]],<ref name="Newcomb_1881">{{cite journal|author=Newcomb, S.| title=Note on the frequency of use of the different digits in natural numbers|journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics|Amer. J. Math.]]|year=1881|volume=4|pages=39–40| doi=10.2307/2369148|issue=1|publisher=The Johns Hopkins University Press|jstor=2369148| bibcode=1881AmJM....4...39N}}</ref> and rediscovered in 1938 by [[Frank Benford]].<ref name="Benford_1938">{{cite journal|author=Benford, F.|title=The law of anomalous numbers| journal=[[Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society|Proc. Am. Philos. Soc.]]| volume=78|year=1938|pages=551–572|bibcode=1938PAPhS..78..551B }}</ref> The first rigorous formulation and proof seems to be due to [[Ted Hill (mathematician)|Ted Hill]] in 1988.;<ref name="Hill_1995">{{cite journal|author=Hill, Theodore P.|title=The Significant Digit Phenomenon| journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly|Amer. Math. Monthly]]| volume=102|date=April 1995|pages=322–327|doi=10.2307/2974952 |issue=4|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|jstor=2974952|url=https://digitalcommons.calpoly.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1041&context=rgp_rsr}}</ref> see also the contribution by [[Persi Diaconis]].<ref name="Diaconis_1977">{{cite journal | author=Diaconis, Persi | title=The distribution of leading digits and uniform distribution mod 1 | journal=[[Annals of Probability|Ann. Probab.]] | volume=5 | date=1977 | pages=72–81 | doi=10.1214/aop/1176995891 | issue=1 | publisher=The Institute of Mathematical Statistics | url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aop/1176995891| doi-access=free }}</ref>
*[[Bertrand's ballot theorem]]. This result concerning the probability that the winner of an election was ahead at each step of ballot counting was first published by [[William Allen Whitworth|W. A. Whitworth]] in 1878, but named after [[Joseph Louis François Bertrand]] who rediscovered it in 1887.<ref>{{citation|title=An Introduction to Probability Theory and its Applications, Volume I|first=William|last=Feller|author-link=William Feller|edition=3rd|publisher=Wiley|year=1968|page=69}}.</ref> A common proof uses ''André's reflection method'', though the proof by [[Désiré André]] did not use any reflections.

== Algebra ==

*[[Burnside's lemma]]. This was stated and proved without attribution in Burnside's 1897 textbook,<ref name="Burnside_1897">{{cite book |author=Burnside, William |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.168629 |title=Theory of groups of finite order |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1897}}</ref> but it had previously been discussed by [[Augustin Louis Cauchy|Augustin Cauchy]], in 1845, and by [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius|Georg Frobenius]] in 1887.
*[[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]]. The theorem was first proved in the easy special case of 2×2 matrices by [[Arthur Cayley|Cayley]], and later for the case of 4×4 matrices by [[William Rowan Hamilton|Hamilton]]. But it was only proved in general by [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius|Frobenius]] in 1878.<ref>{{citation |last=Grattan-Guinness |first=Ivor |title=Companion Encyclopaedia of the History and Philosophy of the Mathematical Sciences |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q_1H8WAGmo8C&pg=PA779 |pages=779–780 |year=2002 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=9781134957507}}.</ref>
*[[Hölder's inequality]]. This inequality was first established by [[Leonard James Rogers]], and published in 1888. [[Otto Hölder]] discovered it independently, and published it in 1889.
*[[Marden's theorem]]. This theorem relating the location of the zeros of a complex cubic polynomial to the zeros of its derivative was named by Dan Kalman after Kalman read it in a 1966 book by [[Morris Marden]], who had first written about it in 1945.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Kalman |first1=Dan |title=An Elementary Proof of Marden's Theorem |url=http://mathdl.maa.org/mathDL/22/?pa=content&sa=viewDocument&nodeId=3338&pf=1 |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly|The American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=115 |issue=4 |pages=330–338 |year=2008 |doi=10.1080/00029890.2008.11920532 |issn=0002-9890 |s2cid=13222698}}</ref> But, as Marden had himself written, its original proof was by Jörg Siebeck in 1864.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Siebeck |first1=Jörg |title=Über eine neue analytische Behandlungweise der Brennpunkte |url=http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?PPN=GDZPPN002152495 |journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]] |volume=64 |pages=175–182 |year=1864 |issn=0075-4102}}</ref>
*[[Pólya enumeration theorem]]. This was proven in 1927 in a difficult paper by [[J. Howard Redfield|J. H. Redfield]].<ref name="Redfield_1927">{{cite journal |author=Redfield, J. H. |year=1927 |title=The theory of group related distributions |journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics|Amer. J. Math.]] |publisher=The Johns Hopkins University Press |volume=49 |issue=3 |pages=433–445 |doi=10.2307/2370675 |jstor=2370675}}</ref> Despite the prominence of the venue (the [[American Journal of Mathematics]]), the paper was overlooked. Eventually, the theorem was independently rediscovered in 1936 by [[George Pólya]].<ref name="Pólya_1936">{{cite journal |author=Pólya, G. |year=1936 |title=Algebraische Berechnung der Isomeren einiger organischer Verbindungen |journal=[[Zeitschrift für Kristallographie]] |volume=93 |pages=414 |doi=10.1524/zkri.1936.93.1.415 |s2cid=101816170}}</ref> Not until 1960 did [[Frank Harary]] unearth the much earlier paper by Redfield. See <ref name="Read_1987">{{cite journal |author=Read, R. C. |date=December 1987 |title=Pólya's Theorem and its Progeny |journal=[[Mathematics Magazine]] |volume=60 |issue=5 |pages=275–282 |doi=10.2307/2690407 |jstor=2690407}}</ref> for historical and other information.

== Analysis ==

*[[Frobenius theorem (differential topology)|Frobenius theorem]]. This fundamental theorem was stated and proved in 1840 by [[Feodor Deahna]].<ref name="Deahna_1840">{{cite journal |author=Deahna, F. |year=1840 |title=Über die Bedingungen der Integrabilität |url=https://zenodo.org/record/2312273 |journal=J. Reine Angew. Math. |volume=20 |pages=340–350 |doi=10.1515/crll.1840.20.340 |s2cid=120057555}}</ref> Even though Frobenius cited Deahna's paper in his own 1875 paper,<ref name="Frobenius_1895">{{cite journal |author=Frobenius, Georg |year=1895 |title=Ūber das Pfaffsche Problem |journal=[[Crelle's Journal|J. Reine Angew. Math.]] |pages=230–315}}</ref> it became known after Frobenius, not Deahna. See <ref name="Samelson_2001">{{cite journal |author=Samelson, Hans |date=June–July 2001 |title=Differential Forms, the Early days; or the Stories of Deahna's Theorem and of Volterra's Theorem |journal=Amer. Math. Monthly |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |volume=108 |issue=6 |pages=522–530 |doi=10.2307/2695706 |jstor=2695706}}</ref> for a historical review.
*[[L'Hôpital's rule]]. This rule first appeared in l'Hôpital's book ''[[L'Analyse des Infiniment Petits pour l'Intelligence des Lignes Courbes]]'' in 1696. The rule is believed to be the work of [[Johann Bernoulli]] since l'Hôpital, a nobleman, paid Bernoulli a retainer of 300 francs per year to keep him updated on developments in calculus and to solve problems he had. See [[L'Analyse des Infiniment Petits pour l'Intelligence des Lignes Courbes]] and reference therein.
*[[Maclaurin series]]. The Maclaurin series was named after [[Colin Maclaurin]], a professor in Edinburgh, who published this special case of the [[Taylor series]] in 1742, but never claimed to have discovered it.<ref name="thomas">{{cite book |author=Thomas & Finney |url=https://archive.org/details/calculusanalytic00geor_0 |title=Calculus and Analytic Geometry |publisher=Addison Wesley Publishing Company |year=1996 |url-access=registration}}</ref>
*[[Poincaré lemma]]. This was mentioned in 1886 by [[Henri Poincaré]],<ref name="Poincare_1886">{{cite journal |author=Poincaré, H. |year=1886–1887 |title=Sur les residus des intégrales doubles |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1670438 |journal=[[Acta Mathematica|Acta Math.]] |volume=9 |pages=321–380 |doi=10.1007/BF02406742 |doi-access=free}}</ref> but was first proved in a series of 1889 papers by the distinguished Italian mathematician [[Vito Volterra]]. Nonetheless, it has become known after Poincaré. See <ref name="Samelson_2001" /> for the twisted history of this lemma.
*[[Stokes' theorem]]. It is named after Sir [[George Gabriel Stokes]] (1819–1903), although the first known statement of the theorem is by [[William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin|William Thomson]] (Lord Kelvin) and appears in a letter of his to Stokes. The theorem acquired its name from Stokes' habit of including it in the [[Cambridge University|Cambridge]] prize examinations. In 1854 he asked his students to prove the theorem in an examination; it is not known if anyone was able to do so.<ref name="Katz_1979">{{cite journal |author=Victor J. Katz |author-link=Victor J. Katz |date=May 1979 |title=The History of Stokes' Theorem |journal=[[Mathematics Magazine]] |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=146–156 |doi=10.2307/2690275 |jstor=2690275}}</ref>

== Geometry and topology ==

*[[Ceva's theorem]]. The oldest extant proof can be found in [[Yusuf al-Mu'taman ibn Hud]]'s 11th century ''Kitab al-Istikmal'' (''Book of Perfection''), about six centuries before [[Giovanni Ceva]]'s 1678 ''De lineis rectis'' (''On straight lines'').<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hogendijk |first=Jan P |year=1995 |title=Al-Mu'taman ibn Hūd, 11th century king of Saragossa and brilliant mathematician |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=22 |pages=1–18 |doi=10.1006/hmat.1995.1001 |doi-access=free |number=1}}</ref>
*[[Cramer's paradox]]. This was first noted by [[Colin Maclaurin]] in 1720, and then rediscovered by [[Leonhard Euler]] in 1748 (whose paper was not published for another two years, as Euler wrote his papers faster than his printers could print them). It was also discussed by [[Gabriel Cramer]] in 1750, who independently suggested the essential idea needed for the resolution, although providing a rigorous proof remained an outstanding open problem for much of the 19th century. Even though Cramer had cited Maclaurin, the paradox became known after Cramer rather than Maclaurin. [[Georges Henri Halphen|Georges Halphen]], [[Arthur Cayley]], and several other mathematicians contributed to the earliest more or less correct proof. See <ref name="Scott_1898">{{cite journal |author=Scott, Charlotte Agnas |date=March 1898 |title=On the Intersection of Plane Curves |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|Bull. Am. Math. Soc.]] |volume=4 |issue=6 |pages=260–273 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1898-00489-5 |doi-access=free}}</ref> for an excellent review.
*[[Heine–Borel theorem]]. This theorem was proved in 1872 by [[Émile Borel]], not by [[Eduard Heine]]. Borel used techniques similar to those that Heine used to prove that continuous functions on closed intervals are uniformly continuous. Heine's name was attached because [[Arthur Moritz Schönflies|Schönflies]] noticed the similarity in Heine's and Borel's approaches. In fact, the theorem was first proved in 1852 by [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]], but Lejeune Dirichlet's lecture notes were not published until 1904.<ref name="Sundstrom_2010">{{cite arXiv |eprint=1006.4131v1 |class=math.HO |first=Manya Raman |last=Sundström |title=A pedagogical history of compactness |year=2010 |page=7}}</ref>
*Models of hyperbolic geometry. "By one of the injustices of nomenclature that are so common in mathematics, the three models – which could appropriately be called Riemann-Beltrami, Liouville-Beltrami, and Cayley-Beltrami models – are usually known as the [[Poincaré disk model]], the [[Poincaré half-plane model]] and the [[Klein disk model]]."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stillwell |first1=John |author-link1=John Stillwell |title=Sources of hyperbolic geometry |date=1996 |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] and [[London Mathematical Society]] |location=Providence, R.I. and London |isbn=0-8218-0529-0 |page=35 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZQjBXxxQsucC&pg=PA35}}</ref>
*[[Morrie's law]]. The name is due to physicist [[Richard Feynman]], who used to refer to the identity under that name. Feynman picked that name because he had learned the law during his childhood from a boy with the name Morrie Jacobs.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Beyer |first1=W. A. |last2=Louck |first2=J. D. |last3=Zeilberger |first3=D. |author-link3=Doron Zeilberger |title=Math Bite: A Generalization of a Curiosity that Feynman Remembered All His Life |journal=[[Mathematics Magazine]] |date=February 1996 |volume=69 |issue=1 |pages=43–44 |doi=10.1080/0025570X.1996.11996378 |jstor=2691393}}</ref>
*[[File:Plimpton 322.jpg|thumb|Plimpton 322, a tablet that contained several Pythagorean triples]][[Pythagorean theorem|Pythagoras' theorem]]. This was known to ancient [[Mesopotamia]]n mathematicians over one thousand years before Pythagoras was born.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Joran |first1=Friberg |title=Methods and traditions of Babylonian mathematics: Plimpton 322, Pythagorean Triples, and the Babylonian Triangle Parameter Equations |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222892801 |journal=Historia Mathematica |doi=10.1016/0315-0860(81)90069-0 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Number theory ==
*[[Bézout's theorem]]. The statement may have been made first by [[Isaac Newton]] in 1665. The matter of a proof was taken up by [[Colin MacLaurin]] (c. 1720) and [[Leonhard Euler]] as well as [[Étienne Bézout]] (c. 1750). However, Bézout's "proof" was ''incorrect''. The first correct proof seems to be due mostly to [[Georges-Henri Halphen]] in the 1870s.<ref name="Bix_1998">{{cite book|author=Bix, Robert|title=Conics and Cubics|url=https://archive.org/details/conicscubicsconc0000bixr|url-access=registration|publisher=Springer| year=1998|isbn=0-387-98401-1}}</ref>
*[[Cramer's rule]]. It is named after [[Gabriel Cramer]] (1704–1752), who published the rule in his 1750 ''Introduction à l'analyse des lignes courbes algébriques'', although [[Colin Maclaurin]] also published the method in his 1748 ''Treatise of Algebra'' (and probably knew of the method as early as 1729).<ref name="Boyer_1968">{{cite book |author=Carl B. Boyer |title=A History of Mathematics, 2nd edition |publisher=Wiley |year=1968 |page=431}}</ref>
*[[Pell's equation]]. The solution of the equation ''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;''dy''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, where ''x'' and ''y'' are unknown positive integers and where ''d'' is a known positive integer which is not a perfect square, is ascribed to [[John Pell (mathematician)|John Pell]]. It seems to have been discovered by [[Pierre de Fermat|Fermat]], who set it as a challenge problem in 1657. The first European solution is found in a joint work in 1658 by [[John Wallis]] and [[Lord Brouncker]]; in 1668, a shorter solution was given in an edition of a third mathematician's work by Pell; see ref.<ref name="Cajori_1999">{{cite book |author=Cajori, Florian |title=A History of Mathematics |publisher=Chelsea |year=1999 |isbn=0-8284-0203-5 |location=New York |author-link=Cajori, Florian}} (reprint of fifth edition, 1891).</ref> The first rigorous proof may be due to [[Joseph Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]]. The misnomer apparently came about when [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]] confused Brouncker and Pell; see <ref name="Whitford_1912">{{cite book |author=Whitford, Edward Everett |url=https://archive.org/details/pellequation00whitgoog |title=The Pell Equation |publisher=E. E. Whitford |year=1912 |location=New York}} This is Whitford's 1912 Ph.D. dissertation, written at [[Columbia University]] and published at his own expense in 1912.</ref> for an extensive account of the history of this equation.

== Set theory ==
*[[Zorn's lemma]] is named for [[Max August Zorn|Max Zorn]]. Much work on the theorem now known as Zorn's lemma, and on several closely related formulations such as the [[Hausdorff maximal principle]], was done between 1907 and 1940 by Zorn, [[L. E. J. Brouwer|Brouwer]], [[Felix Hausdorff|Hausdorff]], [[Kazimierz Kuratowski|Kuratowski]], [[R. L. Moore]], and others. But the particular theorem now known as "Zorn's lemma" was never proved by Zorn, and in any event Zorn's results were anticipated by Kuratowski. The theorem was discovered by [[Claude Chevalley|Chevalley]] in 1936, and published and attributed to Zorn by him in Bourbaki's ''Théorie des Ensembles'' in 1939. A very similar result was anticipated by [[Salomon Bochner|S. Bochner]] in 1928.<ref name="Campbell_1978">{{cite journal | journal = [[Historia Mathematica]] | title = The Origin of 'Zorn's Lemma' | last1 = Campbell | first1 = Paul J. | volume = 5 | year = 1978 | pages = 77–89 | doi = 10.1016/0315-0860(78)90136-2 | doi-access =  }}</ref>
